channel.title: HAT MI Daily - Macro and Industries
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Japan's core consumer prices, excluding fresh food, rose 2.2% year on year in October, up from 2.1% in September and above the Bank of Japan's 2% target for a second month, as markets expect a December rate rise.
item.description:
Japan's core consumer price index, which excludes volatile fresh food, rose 2.2% year on year in October after 2.1% in September, above the central bank's 2% target for the second consecutive month, CNA reports; Commercial Times adds that it was 1.7% in August and slightly below the 2.3% forecast by economists surveyed by Bloomberg. An index that excludes both fresh food and fuel, which the Bank of Japan watches as a better gauge of demand-driven price pressure, rose 2.2% after 2.4% in September. Capital Economics' Marcel Thieliant expects inflation excluding fresh food and energy to accelerate sharply in the coming months as companies continue to pass on rising raw material costs. Commercial Times reports that the Bank of Japan said last month inflation had reached its target and expected it to be "significantly above 2%" in the coming months, driven by price rises across goods and services including semiconductors, and that the market expects a rate rise in December. The rows do not give the date of the December meeting.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The core rate excluding fresh food rose while the index excluding both fresh food and fuel slowed from 2.4% to 2.2%, which points to energy rather than underlying prices behind the October rise. The Mainichi reports energy prices rose 2.2% from a year earlier after a 0.6% fall in September. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a Bank of Japan rate rise would tend to support the yen and raise borrowing costs for Japanese companies and households. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, a stronger yen would lower the cost of imported raw materials for producers in Japan and change the price position of Japanese exporters in cars and electronics, which are major customer industries. Points that may be worth considering include the Bank of Japan's December decision, the yen, and the pass-through of raw material costs reported by Japanese manufacturers.

CNA | Commercial Times | The Mainichi

item.title: South Korea's exports passed USD 1 trillion on 19 November, against a record USD 709 billion last year, the trade ministry says, and CNA reports the rise was led by semiconductors while autos, steel and ships lagged.
item.description:
South Korea's exports passed the USD 1 trillion mark on 19 November, compared with a record USD 709 billion last year, according to the country's trade ministry, CNA reports. This makes South Korea the fourth country to reach the milestone, after Germany, the United States and China. The rise has been led by semiconductors as AI investment drives demand: chip exports jumped 184% year on year in the first three quarters of 2026 and accounted for 42% of total exports, more than double their average 20% share over the past five years. Traditional manufacturing sectors such as autos, steel and ships have lagged amid protectionism triggered by US tariffs and geopolitical conflicts such as the Iran war. The row does not give export values for autos, steel or ships, or import figures.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The total is led by one sector: chips' share of exports more than doubled against the five-year average, while the other main sectors lagged. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a record total driven by chip prices and volumes says little about the condition of Korea's car, steel and shipbuilding industries. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, Korean chip and electronics output supports demand for semiconductor and electronics materials, while the lag in autos, steel and ships points to weaker demand in those Korean end-markets. Points that may be worth considering include Korea's full-year car and steel exports, chip export growth in the fourth quarter, and US tariff decisions affecting Korean goods.

CNA

item.title: The IEA says the energy crisis from the Iran war will leave lasting marks on the world's energy sector, and its World Energy Outlook 2026 finds that demand for cooling buildings is overtaking demand for heating for the first time.
item.description:
According to the International Energy Agency report, energy-hungry nations will prioritise the security and affordability of their electricity, which supports solar and nuclear but also reinforces the case to keep coal as a backup in times of crisis, especially in coal-rich Asia, which went into energy triage when the Iran war cut off the Strait of Hormuz, AP reports. Anadolu Agency reports the outlook finds global demand for cooling buildings overtaking heating for the first time, citing rising temperatures and household incomes. Outside China, 85% of households in emerging and developing economies face high temperatures, yet fewer than one in five has an air conditioner. Under the IEA's Stated Policies Scenario, electricity use for cooling is projected to rise by 1,700 terawatt-hours by 2035, and more intense heat waves could raise that to about 2,400 terawatt-hours, about 40% above the projection. LiveMint reports the IEA expects India to lead global oil demand growth, with consumption rising by an average of 3% a year to 2035, adding 1.3 million barrels a day under the same scenario. The rows do not give the outlook's price assumptions or figures for Europe.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The outlook consists of projections and scenarios, not measured outcomes. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a lasting priority on energy security and affordability shifts investment towards power grids, solar, nuclear and cooling equipment, and keeps oil demand growth concentrated in emerging economies such as India. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, air conditioners, solar modules, grid equipment and building insulation use bonding, sealing and thermal management materials, so growth in cooling demand in emerging economies points to demand in those applications. Points that may be worth considering include the outlook's figures for Europe, its energy price paths, and how far the coal-backup case reported for Asia shapes power investment.

AP | Anadolu Agency | LiveMint

item.title: Cement from outside the EU made up 29.3% of UK cement imports in January–September, up from 17.1% a year earlier, which the Mineral Products Association links to trade re-routing after the EU's carbon border levy.
item.description:
An analysis of HMRC figures by the Mineral Products Association (MPA) shows importers are re-routing cement to the UK in the wake of European carbon border regulations, with non-European imports at their highest level since records began in 2000. The MPA says the data suggest cement trade flows are being diverted following the introduction of the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) at the start of 2026. Cement from outside the EU accounted for 29.3% of UK cement imports in January–September 2026, up sharply from 17.1% in the same period of 2025. The row does not give import volumes, prices or countries of origin.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The 29.3% is a share of imports, not a volume, and the row does not say how large imports are relative to UK cement use. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, the CBAM puts a charge on the carbon emitted in producing certain imports into the EU, including cement, so higher-carbon cement that would have gone to the EU can move to nearby markets without a comparable charge. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, cement is a base material for tile adhesives, mortars and screeds, so a larger share of imported cement can affect UK building-material costs and the reported carbon footprint of construction products. Points that may be worth considering include import volumes and origins, whether the UK introduces a comparable carbon border charge, and similar re-routing in other markets outside the EU.

Mineral Products Association

item.title: The presidents of the US, China and Russia issued a joint "Declaration toward Peace" after their first face-to-face trilateral meeting, in Shenzhen, which includes a plan to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products.
item.description:
The China-Russia-U.S. Heads of State Declaration toward Peace was issued on 19 November by Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump after their summit in Shenzhen, MarketScreener reports. As permanent members of the UN Security Council, the three countries pledged to promote reform of the United Nations, plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations, and reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows. People's Daily reports it was the first face-to-face meeting of the three heads of state. BBC News reports the three presidents also agreed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought, and that the International Criminal Court and similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction. Asharq Al-Awsat reports that refining industry data show different constraints in each country: high refinery utilisation in the United States, declining crude processing in China and damage to Russian refineries from the war in Ukraine. The Daily Mail reports that the meeting lasted roughly an hour and a half and ended without any major agreements; it does not say how it views the declaration. The rows do not give volumes, timing, product types or a mechanism for the supply increase.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The supply point is a stated plan, the rows give no volumes, and Asharq Al-Awsat reports different refining constraints in each of the three countries. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, refined products such as diesel and naphtha set fuel and petrochemical feedstock costs, and a coordinated supply increase by the three countries would matter for those costs only once volumes or export measures follow. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, many polymers, resins and solvents come from refinery and petrochemical streams, so the declaration by itself does not change cost expectations. Points that may be worth considering include any announced volumes or export measures, diesel and naphtha price moves, and follow-up talks on the war in Ukraine.

MarketScreener | People's Daily | BBC News | Asharq Al-Awsat | The Daily Mail

item.title: The Global Electronics Association has issued an industry alert on escalating shortages across the printed circuit board supply chain, saying AI absorbs scarce capacity and that availability, not price, is the real risk facing the industry.
item.description:
The Global Electronics Association, which describes itself as the voice of the electronics industry, says companies in automotive, industrial, medical, defence and telecommunications report longer lead times and difficulty securing supply of printed circuit boards (PCBs) as AI absorbs scarce capacity, effectively putting production at risk. It sets out its case in an explanatory report, "PCB Squeeze: A Wake-Up Call for Global Electronics". The rows do not quantify lead times, capacity or prices, name the regions affected, or say which stages of the PCB supply chain are tightest.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

This is an alert from an industry association, not a measurement. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, when AI servers take priority in board capacity, other electronics users wait longer, which can delay production of vehicles and industrial equipment. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, circuit-board assembly uses conformal coatings, underfills and thermally conductive materials, so a capacity squeeze can shift board volumes towards AI hardware and can slow volumes in automotive and industrial electronics, with lead times rather than prices shaping customers' purchasing. Points that may be worth considering include lead-time data, any figures in the association's report, and whether carmakers or industrial producers report production effects.

Financial Post | AP

item.title: Japan's carmakers will standardise vehicle materials and parts, starting with steel, resins and wire harnesses, to cut procurement costs and strengthen competitiveness against overseas rivals, the industry association JAMA says.
item.description:
On 19 November the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association (JAMA) announced that Japanese automakers will standardise vehicle materials and parts, starting with steel, resins and wire harnesses, to strengthen the industry's competitive edge against overseas rivals, Japan Today reports. Through cooperation across manufacturers, the association aims to gradually expand the range of standardised parts and materials to cut procurement costs. For steel, it will standardise the types of steel sheets; for resins, it will align recycling-related evaluation criteria that currently vary among automakers. JAMA plans to work with the Japan Auto Parts Industries Association. According to the report, the move could help suppliers win higher-volume orders, but it may also intensify price competition by making it difficult for companies to differentiate their products. The row does not name the participating carmakers, give a timetable, say which resin types are covered, or quantify the expected cost saving.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

This is a plan announced by an industry association, and the row gives no timetable or volumes. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, common specifications across carmakers concentrate demand on fewer approved grades and shift competition among material suppliers towards price and scale, which is the trade-off the report itself describes. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, bonding and sealing products are usually qualified against specific substrates, so common recycling criteria for resins could change which plastics are used in vehicle parts and how many approvals a supplier needs; bonding and sealing products are not named in the row. Points that may be worth considering include which materials follow steel, resins and wire harnesses, the timetable, and whether the parts suppliers' association adopts common test criteria.

Japan Today

item.title: Taiwan's manufacturing output value rose 43.09% year on year to a record TWD 7.51 trillion in the third quarter, and the production index, which excludes price effects, rose 23.14%, on demand linked to artificial intelligence.
item.description:
Taiwan's Ministry of Economic Affairs' Department of Statistics said on 19 November that third-quarter manufacturing output value reached TWD 7.51 trillion, the first quarter above TWD 7 trillion, Commercial Times reports. The year-on-year growth of 43% was the strongest in 16 years. Measured by output volume rather than value, the manufacturing production index rose 23.14% to 145.59, and both output value and the production index have grown for 11 consecutive quarters. The rise is attributed to demand for artificial intelligence applications, investment in the semiconductor industry and spillover demand from the AI supply chain to some traditional industries. All six major manufacturing sectors grew year on year: computers, electronic products and optical products by 129%, electronic components by 52%. Chemical materials and fertilisers, basic metals, and machinery and equipment all grew by double digits, and automobiles and parts recorded the smallest increase, at 1%. The rows do not give a fourth-quarter outlook or split the production index by sector.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The production index, which excludes price factors, rose 23.14% against 43.09% for output value, so price effects account for part, but not most, of the value growth, and automobiles and parts grew only 1%. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, growth led by computers and electronic components is likely to be concentrated in AI servers and chips. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, electronics assembly and semiconductor packaging use underfills, die-attach adhesives and thermal interface materials, so growth of this size in Taiwan's computer and electronic-component output value points to demand for these categories in AI-related products. Points that may be worth considering include fourth-quarter data, the sector split of the production index, and whether the double-digit growth in traditional industries holds.

Commercial Times | Commercial Times

item.title: The share of German firms saying a lack of skilled workers restricts their business fell to 23% in October, three points lower than a year earlier, while among industrial firms it rose 2.5 points to 19.6%, the KfW–Ifo barometer shows.
item.description:
In the skilled-labour barometer of the development bank KfW and the Munich Ifo Institute, 23% of the 9,000 companies surveyed in October said that a lack of qualified personnel was restricting their business activities, Süddeutsche Zeitung and Handelsblatt report. In October of the previous year the figure was three percentage points higher, and the record was nearly 50% in summer 2022. Handelsblatt reports differences between sectors: in retail the share fell from around 22% in October 2025 to around 17%, and among service companies from 30% to 25%. Industry moved against the overall trend: 19.6% of industrial companies reported a shortage of skilled workers, 2.5 percentage points more than in 2025, and construction companies were particularly affected, with 31% saying a lack of skilled workers restricted their business, Handelsblatt reports. The rows do not give reasons for the changes, a regional split, or figures for the chemical industry.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The barometer measures companies' own assessment of a constraint, not vacancies or employment. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a falling share of constrained firms can reflect lower hiring needs in a weak economy as much as a larger supply of workers, and the rows do not say which of the two is behind the fall in the overall October figure. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the easing reported is in retail and services, while the industrial share rose and construction remains the most constrained sector, so on these figures staffing pressure at German production sites and at customers in construction and manufacturing has not eased. Points that may be worth considering include the industrial share in coming months, German employment and order data, and wage settlements in manufacturing.

Handelsblatt | Süddeutsche Zeitung

item.title: Spain's vehicle production fell 10.9% in October to 188,058 units, with passenger cars down 12% and commercial vehicles down 6.5%, manufacturers' association Anfac says.
item.description:
Vehicle production in Spain fell 10.9% to 188,058 units in October, according to the Spanish Association of Automobile and Truck Manufacturers (Anfac), El Correo reports; La Vanguardia, citing the same data, gives the fall as 11%. Passenger car output fell 12% to 145,669 units and commercial vehicles 6.5% to 42,389. La Vanguardia attributes the fall to occasional stoppages caused by operational problems and to weaker demand in the main markets; El Correo to adjustments in the production pace of some plants. Renault's plant in Palencia was shut from 1 to 19 October for lack of orders for its large models, and Renault will drop the night shift at its Valladolid plant at the end of the year. Ford's Almussafes plant had several weeks without activity under a temporary layoff scheme (ERTE) because of low workload, and Seat's Martorell plant had some working days disrupted by a lack of battery cells for electric vehicles. The two outlets give conflicting year-to-date totals, so these are not reported here. The rows do not state the comparison period for the October fall or give a split by plant, powertrain or export market.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Production measures output at Spanish plants, not sales, and the causes reported are partly plant-specific (orders for particular models, a temporary layoff scheme, battery cells) and partly weaker demand in the main markets. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, stoppages tied to orders for specific models and to battery-cell supply suggest that both European demand in some segments and the supply of electric-vehicle components are limiting assembly volumes. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, lower assembly volumes can reduce demand for the structural bonding materials and sealants used in body, interior and battery assembly, and a battery-cell shortage can delay electric-vehicle production, which tends to use more bonding per vehicle. Points that may be worth considering include November production data, whether the Valladolid night-shift cut goes ahead at year-end and the Almussafes layoff scheme continues into 2027, and battery-cell supply to Spanish plants.

El Correo | La Vanguardia
